verdicts.text: According to Mordor Intelligence, the global Kubernetes market is valued at USD 3.13 billion in 2026 and is projected to reach USD 8.41 billion by 2031, a 21.85% CAGR.
verdicts.evidence: cited URL returns HTTP 403 (Forbidden) with an empty body, so none of the figures (USD 3.13B in 2026, USD 8.41B by 2031, 21.85% CAGR) could be checked against the source.
verdicts.framing_note: No source body was fetched, so the framing check couldn't be run.
verdicts.intuition_flag: A 403 from Mordor Intelligence is probably bot-blocking rather than a dead link. A person should load the page in a browser to confirm the figures before treating this as a broken citation.

verdicts.text: CNCF's Q3 2025 report says 30% of backend developers use Kubernetes directly, down from a peak of 36% in Q3 2023, a decline the report attributes to the technology's growing maturity.
verdicts.evidence: The cited PDF returned HTTP 200, but the pre-fetched body is compressed binary PDF streams (fonts and images) with no text I could read. I couldn't find any passage that confirms or refutes the 30% vs. 36% figures or the maturity explanation.
verdicts.framing_note: Couldn't run the framing check because the PDF body had no readable text. A reviewer should check whether the report itself names 'growing maturity' as the cause, or whether that explanation is the author's gloss.
verdicts.intuition_flag: The causal part ('a decline the report attributes to the technology's growing maturity') is where an author's reading most often gets pinned on the source. The figures may be right while the explanation is added.

verdicts.text: Inference workloads powered by LLMs and GPUs now require low-latency execution closer to the user, pushing organizations to schedule AI pipelines across edge and core clusters, often using Kubernetes as the common control plane.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) An arXiv paper (LMEdge, 2026) says "LLM services increasingly operate on edge infrastructure, enabling low-latency and privacy-preserving AI services," and tests this on a Kubernetes edge testbed. A 2026 DEV Community post says enterprises are putting LLM workloads on Kubernetes and "pushing inference to the edge" to meet latency targets. Both back the general trend, but neither is an authoritative industry survey.
verdicts.framing_note: No source is cited. This is a broad, qualitative trend claim ("often using Kubernetes"), and only research and blog sources back it.
verdicts.intuition_flag: "Now require" is stronger than the evidence, which shows edge LLM inference is a growing trend rather than a universal requirement. Also, the post's title is about 2024, but the line reads like 2026-era content.

verdicts.text: Pulumi published a comparison of Kubernetes IaC tools at /blog/best-kubernetes-iac-tools-2026/.
verdicts.evidence: Wrong page fetched: the claim names /blog/best-kubernetes-iac-tools-2026/, but the pre-fetched page is /blog/beyond-yaml-kubernetes-2026-automation-era/. The truncated body of that page is navigation text only and says nothing about whether the best-kubernetes-iac-tools-2026 post exists.
verdicts.framing_note: The fetched URL is not the URL the claim names, so no framing check was run.
verdicts.intuition_flag: A 2024 trends post links to a post with 2026 in its slug. Check that content/blog/best-kubernetes-iac-tools-2026/ exists in the repo.

verdicts.text: AI-powered coding assistants like GitHub Copilot, Claude Code and Cursor have moved from novelty to everyday tooling for a large share of enterprise software teams.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) Several independent survey roundups back up the qualitative claim. The Stack Overflow 2025 survey found "51% of professional developers use AI tools daily", and JetBrains 2025 found 85% using AI tools regularly with 62% relying on at least one assistant. Enterprise uptake is also reported as high ("90% of Fortune 100 companies use GitHub Copilot"). JetBrains Jan 2026 data puts Copilot at 29% and Cursor and Claude Code at 18% each for use at work.
verdicts.framing_note: The claim is vague ("a large share of enterprise software teams") and cites no source. The surveys measure individual developers, not teams, but they strongly support the qualitative trend.

verdicts.text: According to Gartner, by 2028, 75% of enterprise software engineers will use dedicated AI code assistants, and 63% of organizations are currently piloting, deploying or beginning to use AI code assistants.
verdicts.evidence: Gartner's April 11, 2024 press release backs both numbers: "By 2028, 75% of enterprise software engineers will use AI code assistants" and "Sixty-three percent of organizations are currently piloting, deploying or have already deployed AI code assistants." But the claim changes "have already deployed" to "beginning to use" and adds the word "dedicated", which the source doesn't use.
verdicts.framing_note: shifted: the source says "piloting, deploying or have already deployed" and the claim says "piloting, deploying or beginning to use", which understates mature deployment. The claim also adds "dedicated" to "AI code assistants". "Currently" refers to a Q3 2023 survey.

verdicts.text: The July 2026 revision of the Model Context Protocol is described by its maintainers as the largest revision of the protocol to date.
verdicts.evidence: The cited page (HTTP 200) is the lead maintainers' post on the 2026-07-28 spec. It says "we're officially pushing the release button on the next version of the MCP specification, 2026-07-28" and calls the stateless core "The highlight of this release". The fetched body was cut off, and nothing in the part I could read says this is the "largest revision" of the protocol.
verdicts.framing_note: I couldn't find a passage backing "largest revision to date" in the fetched part of the page, so there was nothing to run the framing check against. The claim may overstate the post's wording ("next version", "highlight of this release").
verdicts.intuition_flag: The superlative "largest revision to date" may be the author's own description, not the maintainers'. Check the rest of the page before publishing.

verdicts.text: The July 2026 MCP revision is part of what makes direct action by AI assistants on infrastructure practical.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) A July 2026 MCP revision did ship. The official blog says "The 2026-07-28 Model Context Protocol specification is out, bringing a stateless protocol core, Multi Round-Trip Requests, header-based routing, cacheable list results, authorization hardening..." The Tasks extension (long-running work) and the stronger authorization reasonably support the editorial point that agents can act directly on infrastructure, but no source makes that exact causal link.
verdicts.framing_note: The factual anchor (a July 2026 MCP spec revision) is confirmed. The "makes direct action on infrastructure practical" part is the author's own reading of it, not something a source states.
verdicts.intuition_flag: The post's slug says "2024-and-beyond" but it cites a July 2026 spec. Check that the date framing fits the rest of the updated post.

verdicts.text: Mirantis's Lens has launched a built-in MCP server connecting AI coding assistants to Kubernetes.
verdicts.evidence: The cited Mirantis press page returns HTTP 200 with the title "Lens Launches Built-In MCP Server | Mirantis". Its URL slug reads "lens-launches-built-in-mcp-server-connecting-ai-coding-assistants-to-kubernetes". The fetched body was cut off before the article text, so the title and slug are the only evidence.
verdicts.framing_note: The claim repeats the press release's title and slug, "Lens Launches Built-In MCP Server ... connecting AI coding assistants to Kubernetes".

verdicts.text: As enterprise adoption of AI assistants increases, expectations are rising: they must not only generate code but also understand the state of infrastructure, configurations, and security posture. That means being able to answer questions about environments, surface misconfigurations, or act directly
verdicts.evidence: The cited page loaded (HTTP 200), but it's the MCP 2026-07-28 spec release post. It covers protocol changes such as "a stateless protocol core, Multi Round-Trip Requests, header-based routing" and SDK download counts ("close to half-a-billion downloads a month"). The part we could read says nothing about enterprise adoption of AI assistants or rising expectations that they understand infrastructure state and security posture.
verdicts.framing_note: The page doesn't address the claim. It's about MCP spec features, not enterprise expectations for AI assistants.
verdicts.intuition_flag: This is a general trend statement with no figure, yet it was tagged "numerical". It reads more like editorial opinion than a checkable fact. Also, a post titled for "2024 and beyond" cites a July 2026 spec release as support, which is an odd fit.

verdicts.text: AWS shipped a general-availability MCP server for its Agent Toolkit.
verdicts.evidence: The cited page (HTTP 200) is titled "The AWS MCP Server is now generally available", which confirms the GA claim. The body was cut off before the announcement text, so the only link to the Agent Toolkit I could see is in the site navigation ("Give AI coding agents up-to-date docs and AWS resource access" / "Agent Toolkit"). I could not quote the announcement itself tying the server to the Agent Toolkit.
verdicts.framing_note: Source title: 'The AWS MCP Server is now generally available'. The claim adds 'for its Agent Toolkit', and the fetched text only supports that through site navigation.

verdicts.text: Pulumi Agent Skills is a collection of infrastructure expertise packaged for AI coding assistants, teaching tools such as Claude Code, Cursor, or Gemini CLI to reason about Pulumi projects.
verdicts.evidence: The cited blog post, found in the local repo, says: "we are releasing Pulumi Agent Skills, a collection of packaged expertise that teaches any AI coding assistant how to work with Pulumi the way an experienced practitioner would." It also says the skills "work across multiple AI coding platforms including Claude Code, GitHub Copilot, Cursor, VS Code, Codex, and Gemini CLI."
verdicts.framing_note: The claim is a close paraphrase of the source: "collection of packaged expertise that teaches any AI coding assistant" matches "collection of infrastructure expertise packaged for AI coding assistants, teaching tools such as Claude Code, Cursor, or Gemini CLI".

verdicts.text: Pulumi has a Remote MCP Server that provides infrastructure access to AI assistants, and Pulumi Neo executes actions with previews, policies, and orchestration.
verdicts.evidence: The cited post says: "We're excited to announce the Pulumi Remote MCP Server—a hosted service that brings AI-powered infrastructure management to any AI assistant that supports the Model Context Protocol" and describes handing tasks off to Neo. The Neo docs back up the previews/policies part: Neo "adds organizational context, policy guardrails, human-in-the-loop approvals" and "Runs previews before anything lands... surface policy violations."
verdicts.framing_note: The cited blog post confirms the Remote MCP Server and Neo's multi-step workflow. The claim that Neo runs "previews, policies" comes from the Neo docs, not the cited post. "Orchestration" loosely matches the post's "multi-step planning"/"managing the entire workflow".

verdicts.text: Modern IaC, unified governance, reusable components, and policy frameworks are all core capabilities of the Pulumi Cloud platform.
verdicts.evidence: This is a broad marketing summary, and Pulumi does offer each capability named. The pricing matrix mentions IaC resources, "[component resources](/docs/iac/concepts/components) which are groupings of resources", and Discovery time "spent on discovery and policy execution". The blog also links Pulumi Policies/Insights governance products (/docs/insights/policy/, /product/insights-governance/). One gap: IaC and components come from the open-source Pulumi engine used together with Pulumi Cloud, not from Pulumi Cloud alone.
verdicts.intuition_flag: Calling IaC and reusable components 'Pulumi Cloud' capabilities blurs the line between the open-source IaC engine and the SaaS platform.
